notes.meaning: God pauses after displaying His wonders in nature and speaks directly to Job. He asks if the one who criticizes Him is really ready to debate the Almighty and answer His questions. God shows Job that anyone who complains against divine rule is acting as though they could teach their Maker how to run the universe.

Job responds not with an argument, but with humbled silence. He admits that he is small, unworthy, and has nothing to say in his own defense. He had complained more than once before, but now he covers his mouth and promises not to speak foolishly again.

The Lord speaks again out of the storm wind, because Job's humbling is not yet complete. He tells Job to stand up like a strong man and get ready for another round of questions. God intends to teach Job that true humility means submitting fully to God's wise rule, not just keeping silent.

God asks Job if he will try to overturn divine justice just to prove himself right. In his pain, Job had spoken as if God were treating him unfairly. God shows him that trying to clear one's own name by blaming the Lord is a dangerous mistake.

The Lord asks Job if he has an arm as strong as God's, or a voice that can thunder like His. An arm represents mighty power, and thunder represents God's commanding voice. If Job cannot match God in strength or authority, he has no right to question how God rules.

God challenges Job to put on royal robes of splendor, honor, and majesty if he wants to act as judge. These glorious qualities belong only to the King of the universe. A mortal man cannot take God's throne or govern creation in His place.

The Lord challenges Job to pour out his anger, spot every arrogant person, and crush wicked rulers on the spot. He tells Job to bury them in the dirt and wrap them in the darkness of the grave, the way criminals are covered before execution. Only God has the supreme power to defeat all human pride and judge evil completely.

God says that if Job can actually bring down the proud and rule the world with justice, then God will admit Job can save himself. But since no human has such power, people cannot save themselves from trouble or from God's judgment. Salvation belongs to the Lord alone, and humans must rely entirely on His grace.

God points Job to a giant beast named Behemoth, reminding Job that He created this animal just as He created man. Even though this creature is immense and terrifyingly strong, it eats grass peacefully like an ox. God shows His care by making such a giant beast a plant-eater rather than a violent predator.

differ.view: Behemoth describes a large dinosaur such as a sauropod, which lived alongside humans before becoming extinct.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Behemoth is either the hippopotamus viewed poetically, or a mythical chaos monster paired with Leviathan from ancient Near Eastern legends.

notes.meaning: The Lord highlights the creature's immense physical frame, from the dense muscles of its belly to its powerful thighs. Its tail moves with the strength of a tall cedar tree, and its bones are as solid as tubes of bronze and bars of iron. This amazing design displays the boundless strength and skill of the Creator.

Behemoth is called the chief work of God, standing first among land animals in size and strength. Human hunters cannot conquer it, but its Maker can easily bring His sword against it. The One who gives life to such a monster can end its life whenever He chooses.

The hills provide plenty of grass and plants for Behemoth to eat. Because it does not hunt for meat, other wild animals are not afraid of it and play freely nearby. This highlights how peaceful God made this mighty giant toward its neighbors.

The beast rests comfortably under thorny lotus plants and hides in the reeds and mud of the marsh. The shade trees and the willows growing by the stream shelter it from the heat. God provided a safe and restful home perfectly suited for this massive creature.

Even when a river floods violently, Behemoth does not panic, but stands calm as the water rushes against its mouth. No human can easily trap it in the open or pierce its nose with a snare. God's point to Job is clear: if man cannot master this fellow creature, how could he ever challenge the God who made it?
